title: Potato vs. sweet potato: nutrition differences

seo.title: Potato vs. sweet potato: nutrition differences
seo.meta_description: Potatoes and sweet potatoes are very similar in calories and carbs. Orange sweet potatoes stand out for beta-carotene; potatoes are strong potassium sources.
seo.search_intent: Compare potato and sweet potato for calories, carbs, fiber, potassium, and vitamins without treating one as universally healthier.

excerpt: Potatoes and sweet potatoes are much closer in calories than their reputations suggest: cooked without added fat, both are roughly 85–95 calories and about 20–21 g carbohydrate per 100 g. Orange sweet potatoes stand out for beta-carotene and usually a little more fiber, while potatoes can provide as much or more potassium. Cooking method matters more than the small calorie difference.
content_html:
Sweet potatoes are often treated as the automatically healthier alternative to white potatoes. That is too simple. When they are cooked in similar ways, their calories and carbohydrate are remarkably close. The more interesting differences are in specific micronutrients.

Calories are nearly a tie

Using simple preparations without added oil, an approximate 100 g comparison looks like this:

Per 100 g cookedPotatoOrange sweet potato
Calories~87–93 kcal~90 kcal
Carbohydrate~20–21 g~21 g
Protein~2 g~2 g
Fiber~1.8–2.2 g~3 g
Potassium~380–500 mg~450–480 mg

There is no meaningful energy gap that makes sweet potato a “diet” version of potato. A 200 g serving of either is around 180 calories before butter, oil, or sauce.

Orange sweet potatoes stand out for beta-carotene

The orange color comes largely from carotenoids, especially beta-carotene, which the body can convert into vitamin A. A normal serving of orange sweet potato can easily provide more than a full day's vitamin A requirement.

That does not apply equally to every sweet potato. White and purple varieties have different pigment profiles, so flesh color gives a clue to which compounds dominate.

White potatoes are not nutritionally empty

Potatoes provide potassium, vitamin C, and vitamin B6. Depending on variety and preparation, their potassium content can match or exceed sweet potato. Calling them “just starch” misses a meaningful part of their nutrient profile.

Sweet potatoes usually contain a little more fiber

A difference of about 1 g fiber per 100 g is useful but not dramatic. At 200 g, that could mean roughly 6 g fiber from sweet potato versus around 4 g from potato.

Eating the edible skin can increase fiber in both.

Sweet taste does not mean dramatically more sugar

During cooking, some sweet-potato starch can be converted into sugars, and certain varieties develop considerable sweetness because of enzyme activity. Even so, most of the carbohydrate remains starch.

A sweeter taste therefore does not make sweet potato nutritionally comparable to a sugary dessert.

Cooking method can create a much bigger difference

Boiled potato and baked sweet potato without oil are close in calories. Deep-frying either can push energy density far above 250 calories per 100 g because of absorbed oil.

Butter, cream, cheese, sugar, and sauces can also change the final dish much more than the tuber's original calorie difference.

Which one should you choose?

Orange sweet potato has a clear advantage in beta-carotene/vitamin A and generally a little more fiber. White potato is an excellent potassium source and contributes vitamin C, with almost the same calories.

The useful conclusion is not to replace one permanently with the other. Use both for variety. They are close in energy but complementary in micronutrients.

faq.question: Which has more calories, potato or sweet potato?
faq.answer: Cooked without added fat, they are very similar—usually around 85–95 calories per 100 g.

faq.question: Does sweet potato have more fiber?
faq.answer: Usually a little more: roughly 3 g per 100 g versus around 2 g in cooked potato.

faq.question: Why is orange sweet potato so high in vitamin A?
faq.answer: Because it is rich in beta-carotene, a carotenoid the body can convert into vitamin A.
